text: how does treams-rs handle multithreading/processing across different hardware configurations?

items.html:
treams-rs only runs on the CPU, using threads on one machine. All of its parallel work, including the dense linear algebra, runs in one shared Rayon thread pool. It never inspects the hardware itself. It adjusts to a machine in two ways: how many threads that pool has, and one rule that limits how many of them a matrix factorization uses.

One pool for everything

  • Pool size: Rayon's global pool takes its size from RAYON_NUM_THREADS. If that isn't set, it uses the number of logical CPUs the process may use, which on Linux respects CPU affinity and container CPU limits. treams-rs never creates its own pool and has no thread-count setting.
  • Linear algebra uses the same pool: dense linear algebra is done by faer, a pure-Rust library built here with Rayon support (crates/treams-core/Cargo.toml:10). I checked faer 0.24.4's source: by default it uses all the threads in Rayon's pool.
  • No second pool: there is no BLAS, LAPACK or OpenMP in the stack, so nothing else competes for cores (docs/benchmarks.md says "This path has no BLAS thread pool").

How work is split

  • Element-wise kernels (Bessel functions, vector waves, polar translations) run in parallel only above a size threshold and otherwise stay serial:
    • special.rs:174 switches at 64 elements.
    • polar.rs:361 switches at 512 or 64 depending on the case, and only if the pool has more than one thread.
    • Each worker gets about four chunks of the work, so chunk size grows or shrinks with the pool.
  • Matrix assembly gives each worker its own block of columns. At tmatrix.rs:579 each worker fills one particle's coupling columns, so no locks are needed.
  • Copying blocks: smatrix.rs:582 copies two sets of blocks in parallel, but only when they have at least 512 rows.
  • Matrix products go through faer using the shared pool (interaction.rs:32 and nearby).

The one hardware-tuned rule: capping LU threads

In crates/treams-core/src/linalg.rs:140-166, LU factorization and its solves are split into many small steps. On large pools, the cost of scheduling those steps outweighed the gain from extra threads.

  • The thread budget is the smaller of faer's setting and the pool size. If faer is set to serial, LU runs serially.
  • With a budget of 4 or fewer, LU uses all of it.
  • Above 4, it uses clamp(min(max(min(rows/512, 4), rows/2048), cols/16), 1, budget). Any solve with fewer than 32 right-hand sides therefore runs serially.
  • It was tuned on a Ryzen 9 9950X with a 16-thread pool, comparing against simply using all 16 threads:
    • 256 rows with 4 right-hand sides went from 47.6 ms to 0.57 ms.
    • 8192 rows with 64 right-hand sides went from 6.5 s to 3.3 s.
  • Above 8192 rows the rule is untested; the docs call it a heuristic, not a measured optimum. A property test (linalg.rs:520) checks that it never exceeds the budget.

The Python boundary

  • GIL: every binding releases Python's global interpreter lock while native code runs, via py.detach(...). Python threads can therefore call in at the same time. They still share the one Rayon pool, so extra Python threads don't add cores.
  • NumPy ufuncs (crates/treams-py/src/ufunc.rs:565-605):
    • Loops go parallel at 1024 elements by default. Some use 64, and trivial ones such as refractive indices never go parallel.
    • All inputs are read into a separate buffer before any output is written, so in-place calls are safe.
    • A panic in the Rust code is caught and raised as a Python exception.

What it doesn't do

  • No hand-written SIMD or CPU-specific builds: treams-rs has no CPU feature detection and no target-cpu build flags (the justfile only remaps source paths). Vector instructions come from the compiler and from faer, which picks them at run time: AVX2/FMA on x86, NEON on ARM. AVX-512 would need faer's nightly feature, which is off.
  • One machine only: no NUMA awareness, no MPI, no multi-process or distributed execution.
  • No GPU on main:
    • CUDA support was moved to the experimental/gpu branch in commit f508135 (now d714d18).
    • The WASM browser build lives on experimental/browser (docs/status.md:17-20).
    • The JAX and PyTorch adapters reject GPU tensors and require CPU float64/complex128 (docs/adapters.md:82-85, 123).
  • Limited hardware coverage:
    • CI runs only on ubuntu-24.04.
    • Performance was measured on a Ryzen 9 9950X (4 threads pinned to CPUs 8–11) and an Apple M3 (4 threads).

Controlling it

  • Set RAYON_NUM_THREADS before the first native call. Rayon builds its pool once per process and it can't be resized afterwards.
  • Restricting the process's CPUs with taskset or a container CPU limit also shrinks the default pool.
  • Limit other thread pools separately: if NumPy/SciPy BLAS or torch run alongside, use threadpoolctl or torch.set_num_threads, because treams-rs doesn't know about their threads. The benchmark harness does this: scripts/benchmark_cluster.py:1606-1624 pins CPU affinity and sets RAYON_, OMP_, MKL_ and OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS to the same value.

Gaps:

  • There's no Python-level setting for thread count.
  • By default the pool uses every logical core, including hyperthreads.
  • The LU rule was tuned on one machine and only up to 8192 rows. On a large many-core server it's worth re-checking with RAYON_NUM_THREADS=N cargo run --release -p treams-core --example benchmark_lu -- <rows> <rhs> <threads> <reps>.

text: ok. i would like to make this really nice, performant, and without footguns. basically the user should never really have to worry about this (with some manual controls if they need to) - how much do you think is missing for that?

items.html:
Quite a lot is missing. The good news is it's mostly layers on top of a sound base, not a rework. Rough size: about 4–6 human dev-weeks (the audit's estimate is 20–28 dev-days) for "no footguns + manual controls". The full bar, including consistent performance and real validation across hardware, is closer to 7–10 weeks. Some of that is machine time on hardware we don't have here.

I ran an 8-area audit in which each finding was rechecked by a skeptical second pass. It kept 77 findings and threw out none outright. I then re-ran the five headline problems myself on the release build. All reproduced.

Already solid

  • One mechanism. treams' parallel code, faer and faer's matrix-multiply kernels all use the same Rayon pool. One pool owned by treams could therefore control everything.
  • No threads until needed. Import starts no threads, and the default pool size respects taskset and container CPU limits.
  • Python concurrency is safe. The GIL is released around native work, and calls from several Python threads gave bitwise-identical results to serial runs.
  • Most results ignore thread count. Forward results, multi-RHS LU, matrix products, GMRES and Cluster.solve() are bitwise identical at any thread count.

Footguns (confirmed)

  1. Forking after any parallel call hangs forever. Fork is the Linux default on every Python version you support (3.12 and 3.13). mp.Pool, ProcessPoolExecutor and torch DataLoader all hang if the parent has already done parallel work, even a 5000-element spherical_jn call. My run: a cold parent was fine, a warm one timed out. RAYON_NUM_THREADS=1 doesn't help.
  2. The interpreter aborts instead of raising MemoryError. Under the same memory limit where NumPy raised MemoryError, cluster_factor exited with code 134, which kills a Jupyter kernel. The error enum has no out-of-memory variant (crates/treams-core/src/lib.rs:60-70).
  3. Gradients aren't reproducible. 12 pullbacks sum floats in an order that depends on thread scheduling. In my run, layer_stack at 4 threads gave 15 distinct gradients in 15 identical calls (differences around 1e-16). That breaks bitwise reproducibility and exact replay of failing property tests, though the values aren't physically wrong.
  4. Eigenvalue order depends on thread count. diff.eig at n=512 returned 410 of 512 eigenvalues in different positions at 1 vs 4 threads; they're returned "in the solver's order" (linalg.rs:388). bands inherits this.
  5. Ufunc reduce/accumulate give wrong answers with threads. The parallel path computes everything before writing any output (crates/treams-py/src/ufunc.rs:578-591), which breaks NumPy's reduction loop. firstbrillouin1d.reduce returned the right answer at 1 thread and 0.5 at 4. This is niche, but it's a silently wrong result.

Controls (missing)

  • No API. There is nothing to read or set the thread count, and threadpoolctl can't see the pool.
  • The count is fixed at the first parallel call. The README's "set before importing" is subtly wrong (it's "before computing").
  • Bad values are silently ignored. RAYON_NUM_THREADS values like "two", "-1" or " 2" silently mean all cores, and "64" gives 64 threads on 4 CPUs, which made eig 12–15× slower.
  • Worker processes oversubscribe. joblib/dask workers set OMP_NUM_THREADS, which treams ignores, so each worker starts a pool the size of the whole machine.

Performance consistency (missing)

  • No central policy for when to go parallel. 32 parallel regions have no size check, and only 3 skip parallelism when the pool has one thread. Small calls pay a 10–130 µs handoff to the pool, even at 1 thread.
  • The LU cap misbehaves at both ends. It uses every thread for any matrix size on pools of 4 or fewer (linalg.rs:144-145), and it forces serial LU at around 768 rows on larger pools.
  • Small eig is slower with threads. eig with no size cutoff is about 1.8× slower at n=256 with 4 threads.
  • Cluster assembly is serial. The main path behind Cluster.solve (basis.rs:139-169) has no parallelism.

Validation (missing)

  • CI never varies the thread count and has no timeouts or fork tests. Several tests split inputs at exactly the parallel cutoff, so both halves take the parallel path and the serial path is never compared.
  • Benchmarks cover one configuration. 1269 of 1300 cases run at exactly 4 threads on one Ryzen. The default setting, SMT, Intel hybrid CPUs, Apple M and Graviton are never measured.

Target design

One pool owned by treams, behind a new treams_core::par module, replacing the ~66 scattered parallel regions:

  • Pool:
    • Built with ThreadPoolBuilder::build, so it can be rebuilt (Rayon's global pool can't be).
    • Checks std::process::id() and builds a fresh pool in a forked child, which fixes the hang.
    • Threads named treams-{i}.
    • Validates the thread count from TREAMS_RS_NUM_THREADS, then RAYON_NUM_THREADS, then OMP_NUM_THREADS, then the CPU count.
  • When to go parallel: should_split/min_len based on an estimated cost per item, and serial inline execution at budget 1 or for small work.
  • Reproducible results: sums use fixed chunks combined in order, and eig/SVD use a fixed parallel split that depends only on problem size. Results are then bitwise identical at any thread count. Eigenvalues get a documented canonical order.
  • Python: get_num_threads, set_num_threads, a threads(n) context manager, thread_info(), and an optional threadpoolctl controller. A lint rule keeps par_iter and friends inside par.rs.

No new Rust dependencies are needed. The suggested order is the fork fix and ufunc fix first, then the par module and controls, then cutoff tuning and calibration.

Caveats

  • Noisy timings. Everything ran on 4 shared vCPUs without SMT. The behavioral results are solid, but timings are rough.
  • Adapters unchecked. JAX and torch weren't installed, so the adapter claims are from reading the code only.
  • Real machines needed. Calibrating cutoffs across hardware needs Intel hybrid, Apple M and Graviton machines.

The full report (evidence with file:line, design, sequenced plan, open questions) is at scratch: final_report.md. I can publish it as a shareable page if you like. I haven't changed or committed anything in either repo.

To start, I'd build the par module with fork-safe pool rebuilding first, since controls, the fork fix and the cutoffs all hang off it. Then the ufunc fix and MemoryError, both small. Want me to start there?

items.html:
The documentation and a baseline implementation are on claude/treams-rs-multithreading-hardware-na6nrm in two commits, 4b53bb6 and 451d100, both pushed. I haven't opened a PR. All checks I ran pass; the gaps are listed under Verification below.

Documentation. docs/parallelism.md is the reference for all of this:

  • User guide: the controls, environment variables, process pools, and which results are reproducible.
  • Design rules: what contributors must keep true.
  • Audit: the findings and a prioritized roadmap with effort estimates.
  • Status: what this branch already fixes.

README.md, docs/status.md and the generated API docs point to it.

Baseline implementation:

  • One pool owned by treams-rs (crates/treams-core/src/par.rs). It is safe across fork, so forking after parallel work no longer hangs. Every parallel region, and every faer call, now runs on it, and Rayon's global pool never starts.
  • Python controls: tr.set_num_threads, with tr.threads(n):, tr.get_num_threads() and tr.thread_info(). The default is read from TREAMS_RS_NUM_THREADS, then RAYON_NUM_THREADS, then OMP_NUM_THREADS, then the CPUs available. Unparsable values now warn instead of silently meaning "all CPUs".
  • Bugs fixed:
    • Ufunc reduce/accumulate gave wrong results with more than one thread.
    • Bessel and angular ufuncs filled only the first output element when every input was a broadcast scalar. This bug predates the branch.
    • vpw_* honored np.errstate only for small arrays.
  • Guards against regressions: a source lint fails if any parallel code is added outside the pool. A check at the end of the test session fails if anything started Rayon's global pool, so new parallel code arriving from the reorganization branches gets caught when it merges.

A review pass turned up several problems, now fixed in the second commit:

  • Tests asked for 3 threads, which would fail on 2-vCPU CI runners.
  • A warning at import broke pytest runs that treat warnings as errors.
  • Benchmark scripts would have been silently overridden by TREAMS_RS_NUM_THREADS.
  • Small dense algebra had started handing work to the pool where it used to run inline.

Behavior changes worth knowing:

  • OMP_NUM_THREADS now sets the treams-rs budget. That makes joblib workers size themselves correctly, but environments that export OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 make treams serial. thread_info() reports this. It's the one open design question; switching it off is a one-line change.
  • The environment is read once at import; use tr.set_num_threads after that.
  • treams-rs no longer reads faer's global parallelism setting.
  • The extension now asks to keep the GIL on free-threaded Python.

Verification:

  • Rust: fmt, Clippy with warnings denied, 100 Rust tests and rustdoc with warnings denied all pass.
  • Python checks: ruff and generated-docs checks pass; strict pyrefly reports 0 errors once jax/torch are installed.
  • Python tests: the full suite passed, 2228 tests. The 68 jax/torch tests skipped there were then run with the extras installed; the adapter suites pass (159 tests).
  • Not run:
    • test_cluster_conditioning_reference.py, which needs mpmath, not installed here.
    • The wheel check and the Lean proofs.
    • GitHub CI status.
    • Any performance measurement of the new pool.

Remaining roadmap. The highest priority is making gradients and eigenvalue order independent of the thread count, and raising MemoryError instead of aborting the process. After that come a central rule for when to go parallel, threadpoolctl integration, and calibrating the size cutoffs on more than one machine.

On the moving target: the wrapping edits are small, local hunks, so conflicts should be simple to resolve.
